Stiff-man syndrome treated with intrathecal
baclofen

Richard D. Penn, MD, and Eugene A. Mangieri, MD

Stiff-man syndrome is a rare, progressive motor disorder caus:
ing disabling muscle rigidity and spasms, which is often associated with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. In patients with
this syndrome, Solimena et al! documented the presence of
autoantibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD)
enzyme scleetively concentrated in pancreatic beta cells
‘CNS neurons secreting the major inhibitory neurotransmitter
amingbutyric acid (GABA). Although plasmapheresis has been
tried.? diazepam remains the most effective treatment; it acts on
the GABA receptors, making: them more sensitive to GABA.*
Unfortunately, as the disoase progresses, diazepam becomes
loss effective and severe spasms occur. Baclofen is a direct
GABA-B agonist that docs not require GABA secretion to aeti-
‘ate its receptor. Thus, baclofen would logically be a useful medication for treating stff-man syndrome if it could be provided
‘sufficiently high concentration to the spinal cord receptors. We
have treated severe spasticity of spinal origin with intrathecal
baclofen and found that it significantly reduces spasms and
rigidity when oral medications failed.” We now report similar
‘success with two patients with stiff man syndrome.

Patient 1. A 42-year old man reported 7 years of progressive
rigidity and spasms that began in hix trunk musculature and
gradually involved both legs and made walking difficult.
Diazepam had afforded initial relief, but as the disease pro:
‘gressod, he became disabled and unable to work at his job as a
machinist. Pain became worse as the intensity and frequency of
‘spasms increased, He gradually clovated his diazepam dose to
140 mg/d, without significant improvement. At age 34, he devel-
‘oped diabetes mellitus and was placed on insulin. His only novrologie abnormalities were demonstrated on motor examination.
He had increased muscle tone in his axial muscles, with a pronounced lumbar lordosis, Mild sensory stimulation or volitional
movements would set off sovere spasms in his back and legs.
His reflexes were normal and Babinski sgn was not present.

‘A lumbar puncture was performed and 75 ug baclofen (Ciba-

,, Basel, Switzerland) was injected. One hour later, his
gidity and spasms completely disappeared and ho was able to
‘walk normally. By 8 hours, the effect was decreasing, and by 24
hhours he returned to baseline. A programmable drug pump and
catheter (Synchro Med, Medtronic, Ine., Minneapolis, MN) going
to the lumbar subarachnoid space was implanted, and hi
‘spasms wore completely controlled with baclofen 120 ygid. Over
tho next 2% years, the dose of intrathecal baclofen was gradually
increased to 1, 200 gid to suppress his spasms; diazepam has
been reduced to 20 mg/d, but is sill necessary in low dose. Ho
thas had an episode of moningitis requiring antibiotics and
replacement of the pump and cathoter system, and twice the
catheter has dislocated from the subarachnoid space and needed
replacement. Each time he stopped receiving intrathecal
‘baclofen his spasms recurred.

Patient 2. A 68-year-old woman was diagnosed with stiff:
‘man xyndrome in 1988. At that time, she had a one-year history
‘of progressive spasms in her back and legs and difficulty with
fit and she required a walker. Pain occurred during attacks of
spasms. On motor examination, she had hyperextension of t
lumbar spine and sovore spasms at the hips and knees, without
‘weaknoss, atrophy, or fasciculations, The reflexes were normal
and a Babinski sign was not prescnt. An extensive work-up was
normal except for antibodies to GAD in her CSF (by Dr.
De Curicelli at Yale University). Diazepam was given and helped
initially, but a year later she was bedridden and having
markedly inereased pain. Intrathecal preservative-froe methylprednisolone and systemic immunotherapy with azathioprine
plasmapheresis were tried without significant effect, By
1992, she had developed ankylosis at her hip, knees, and foet,
secondary atrophy of her leg muscles, and severe pain due to her

spasms. Oral nareoties only provided partial relief, and on
‘numerous oceasions she was admitted for intravenous nareotics..

Intrathecal baclofen was tried, and 75 jg produced excellent
pain relief, stopping the spasms for 4 hours. A drug pump was then
Implanted, with a constant infusion of 120 wai ove the lat 9
months, She has good control af her spasms and pain. She remains
bedridden because of lower-extremity muscle atrophy and ankylosis.

Discussion. Both patients meet the criterion for stiff man
syndrome outlined by Lorish et al.® Dinzepam was initially
effective, but as the disease progressed even high doses (>90 and
>140 mg/d) were inadequate. Since diazepam works by potentiation of the effect of endogenously released GABA on the GABA
receptor, disease progression may reflect lower GABA availability as GABAergic neurons are lost. Baclofen is a direct agonist of
GABA-B receptors and does not require endogenous GABA. This
‘may explain its usefulness in our two patients. Unfortunately,
the second patient developed severe muscle and skeletal
‘changes, and these changes have not reversed. Her major prob Jem of painful spasms hax been controlled. The first patient was
treated earlier in his course and fared better; he continues to do
well ater 2% years of intrathecal baclofen treatment.

Intrathecal baclofen is now approved for the treatment of
‘spasticity of spinal origin, and is available at many centers. On
the basis of our experience with these two patients, wo recom-
‘mend testing patients with stiff man's syndrome with a lumbar
subarachnoid 76-meg baclafon bolus injection when oral diazepam
is no longer providing adequate symptomatic relief. If successful,
‘drug pump can be implanted for chronic administration. If our
‘observations on two patients are confirmed in other patients with
stiff man syndrome, it will be the first example of direct replace-
‘ment of a neurotransmitter by intrathecal infusion,
